content_html:
A family tree needs the number of generations and names defined first. A composition for six people is very different from one for twenty, so decorative branches should not be finalized before the text volume is known.

The search intent requires concrete decisions about scale, color and composition. This guide therefore prioritizes what changes the stitched result rather than offering a generic list of ideas.

Choosing the strongest approach

Scale and detail

Organize hierarchy through branches, levels or visual groups. Each generation should be readable without confusing crossing lines that make relationships ambiguous.

Color and style

Reserve space for long surnames, dates and couples. A flexible lettering system prevents some branches from shrinking to tiny text while others remain mostly empty.

Composition and personalization

The tree can be botanical, geometric or symbolic. Leaves, flowers, frames and small icons should support the family structure rather than hide it.

Rights and accuracy where relevant

For personalization, verify spelling, accents and dates with the customer before generating the final PDF. One incorrect name has major impact in a project that may take weeks to stitch.

Turning it into an original collection

For our catalogue, a base template with genuine layout adaptation makes sense. The value is not replacing twenty names inside one rigid tree but keeping the composition balanced for each family.

In short, the strongest pattern keeps what makes the subject recognizable and removes what only adds noise. That deliberate editing is also the opportunity for our brand: original, clear, stitch-ready patterns rather than images simply passed through a grid.

A family-tree pattern is primarily a layout problem. Before drawing decorative branches, decide how many names and generations the design must hold, whether partners are paired and which dates will appear. A tree that looks balanced with six short names can collapse when a family later adds twelve longer ones, so the text system needs flexibility from the beginning.

Hierarchy should be visible without requiring explanation. Older generations can occupy the roots or lower branches, descendants can spread upward, or the design can use a more neutral circular structure. Whatever metaphor is chosen, keep spacing and typography consistent so relationships remain understandable and no one name appears important merely because it is longer.

Build the lettering at stitch scale. A compact alphabet needs enough height for accents, lowercase if used and clear differences between similar letters. Long surnames may require a wider branch or slightly smaller type, but do not compress them until the characters become ambiguous. Test the longest realistic name before finalizing the template.

Dates add information quickly, so decide whether the product includes birth years, full dates, marriages or no dates at all. More data requires a larger grid. Offering controlled variants—names only, names plus years, or a custom premium layout—can be cleaner than forcing every option into one crowded chart.

Personalization should use a proof stage. The customer must confirm exact spelling, accents, dates and family relationships before the final PDF is generated. Once approved, the preview and chart should be produced from the same data so a corrected name cannot remain wrong on one page.

MAKE can turn family trees into a premium service because the manual layout work is visible and meaningful. The PDF should include finished dimensions and a clean color key, while the product page explains how many names the base format supports and when a larger custom composition is required.

Decide how future additions will work before finalizing a family tree. A design filled completely today may have no place for a new child or generation later. If longevity matters, reserve controlled empty positions or offer an update service that can rebuild the chart while preserving the original style.

Privacy matters in public product previews. Custom mockups used in a portfolio should use permission or anonymized example names and dates rather than automatically publishing a real customer's family information. The final private file and the marketing sample do not need to be identical.

A revision policy should specify when text corrections are free and when structural changes become a new layout. Correcting a typo before approval is different from adding several people after the proof has been accepted. Clear scope protects both premium quality and production time.

Alphabet consistency matters across generations. Do not mix several letter heights just to squeeze long names into awkward spaces; redesign the branch or use a controlled secondary size. The hierarchy should feel intentional rather than patched around individual names.

Color can help hierarchy too: one neutral for branches and a limited accent for names or dates is often clearer than assigning a different shade to every generation. The tree should remain readable even before the text is examined closely.
